newsitem.title: GREECE: Go-slow plays havoc with Greek island flights.
newsitem.headline: Go-slow plays havoc with Greek island flights.

text.p: Dozens of tourists were stranded at Athens airport on Monday in a "go slow" by Olympic Aviation engineers which hit flights to the Greek islands.
Airport officials said at least 20 flights were cancelled or delayed for up to four hours with passengers crammed inside the old airport or standing outside in sizzling heat.
More delays are expected over the next two weeks.

"This is ridiculous. I have been waiting for my flight to be announced for the past three hours. I was hoping to get to an island with my wife and daughter for a nice vacation in Greece but got off to a very bad start," said British tourist Ian Donovan.
"If Greece wants us to come here and spend our money then it should at least make sure it provides basic services like regular flights to tourist locations," his wife Margaret, said.
Olympic Aviation is a subsidiary of the state-owned Olympic Airways serving the popular Aegean Sea islands visited by thousands of tourists each summer.

"The network to the islands is seriously affected by the mechanics' action," a senior government official told Reuters. "It gives Greece a bad name abroad and deals a blow to our efforts to upgrade our tourism services."
The mechanics have banned overtime and demand instead that Olympic, which is deeply in the red, hires more staff.
Olympic Aviation's board was meeting through the day on Monday and officials said that flights to the islands would be reduced over the next two weeks.

Popular island destinations including Paros, Mykonos, Santorini, Skiathos, Zakynthos, Milos and Chios would be affected and hotel owners expressed fears that room reservations from abroad would be cancelled.
The mechanics said that during the busy summer season they are forced to work an average five hours overtime per day under difficult conditions.
A number of foreign carriers warned Greece last summer that they would reduce flights to Athens due to long delays, then caused by an antiquated radar system.
